title: Cruise Control: Controls, Speed Limits and Hill Behavior
introduction: I start with three things: which module controls cruise, where the driver selects its mode, and how road conditions can affect the selected speed. Think of that speed as a target the system works to maintain—even hills get a say in what the speedometer shows. This overview explains those relationships and limits; it is not a complete operating or diagnostic procedure.

edits.text: The PCM (powertrain control module) controls the cruise control system.
edits.why: This identifies the module responsible for managing cruise control.

edits.text: Select the cruise control mode using the steering-wheel-mounted switches labeled ON/OFF, SET+, SET- and CAN/RES. These controls are integrated into the LH (left-hand) steering wheel switch.
edits.why: I use the printed labels to identify the cruise controls within the left-hand switch assembly.

edits.text: Cruise control maintains a selected vehicle speed from 32 km/h (20 mph), or 30 km/h (18 mph) with a metric cluster, up to the vehicle's maximum limited speed. When a MyKey® restricted key is in use and the maximum speed limiter is turned on, vehicle speed is limited to 129 km/h (80 mph).
edits.why: I check the cluster configuration when reading the lower speed threshold. The stated MyKey® limit applies when both conditions are present: a restricted key is in use and the maximum speed limiter is on.

edits.text: During normal driving, road conditions can cause vehicle speed to vary slightly from the set speed. Expect possible fluctuations when driving up and down a steep hill. If vehicle speed drops more than 16 km/h (10 mph) below the set speed, cruise control disengages.
edits.why: A small speed variation can be normal. I distinguish that fluctuation from a drop beyond the stated threshold, because crossing it ends cruise control's active speed control.
